Young Goodman Brown came forth at sunset into the street of Salem village, but he put his head back, after crossing the threshold, to exchange a parting kiss with his young wife. <break time="0.8s" /> And Faith, as the wife was aptly named, thrust her own pretty head into the street, letting the wind play with the pink ribbons of her cap. <break time="0.8s" /> Dearest heart, whispered she, softly and rather sadly, pray tarry with me this night, for a lone woman is troubled with such dreams and thoughts that she is afraid of herself sometimes. <break time="0.8s" /> My love and my Faith, replied Goodman Brown, of all nights in the year, this one night I must stay away from thee, for my journey must be done before sunrise. <break time="0.8s" /> Then he told her to say her prayers and go to bed at dusk, promising that no harm would come to her if she did so. <break time="0.8s" /> As he turned the corner by the meeting house, he looked back and saw the head of Faith still peeping after him with a melancholy air, in spite of her pink ribbons. <break time="0.8s" /> What a wretch am I to leave her, thought he, as his heart smote him, but after this one night I will cling to her and follow her to heaven. <break time="0.8s" /> With this excellent resolve, Goodman Brown hurried onward along a dreary road, darkened by all the gloomiest trees, which barely stood aside to let the narrow path creep through. <break time="0.8s" /> He glanced fearfully behind him, thinking that someone might be hiding behind every tree, or that the devil himself might be at his very elbow.
